e.t: This word means “goodness,” referring to the quality or character of what is good. As a noun, it names goodness rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times across 13 verses, including passages in Judges, Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalms, and Ecclesiastes. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains goodness or good character.

Aedis is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies one individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Genesis 46:16. Because a personal name does not carry a general definition like a common noun or verb, its main function is to identify the person named in the genealogical record. The form Ethis is also given as part of the word’s meaning information.

This adjective means “painful,” describing something that causes or involves pain. It is used three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in Jeremiah: Jeremiah 10:19, 37:12, and 37:13. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided, its precise force in each occurrence cannot be explained further here. Its central idea remains clear: it identifies a person, condition, experience, or circumstance as painful.

This Greek verb means “fill up” or “fulfill.” It describes bringing something to its full measure, completion, or appointed outcome. As a verb, it focuses on the action of making something complete rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 13 times, showing use across several books and settings. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being completed and the surrounding passage.

This verb means “make up; prepare”: it describes getting something ready or arranging it for use. It is an action word, focusing on the work of making something complete or ready rather than merely describing its condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 32 times, with most occurrences in Numbers. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being prepared, but its central sense remains making ready.

This adjective means “endless,” describing something that has no limit or does not come to an end. It presents duration or continuation as unending rather than temporary or finite. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:15. Because the verse text is not included here, the surrounding passage is needed to determine exactly what is described as endless in that occurrence.

This adjective describes someone or something as “ungentle” or “harsh”—lacking gentleness and marked by roughness or severity. It identifies a quality rather than an action, so the surrounding sentence shows what person, behavior, or circumstance has this character. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, both times in Wisdom 17:17–18. Its basic sense remains the same in each occurrence, while the immediate context determines what is being described. The word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “hidden away.” It describes something concealed, kept out of sight, or not openly known. As an adjective, adverb, or noun in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it can identify what is hidden or refer to something kept secret. It occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, including both the Old Testament books and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains concealment rather than open display.

Apollophanes is a proper name—the name of a person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 10:37. Because personal names identify individuals rather than describe an action, quality, object, or relationship, its basic meaning is simply the person’s name. The form “Apollofanis” is another rendering of the same name, not a separate meaning. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain who this individual was or what he did there.

Argob, also rendered Argov, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs four times in this corpus: three times in Deuteronomy and once in 2 Kings. Its precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding passage, but the lexical meaning supplied here is simply the name “Argob” or “Argov.”

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Aroudaios” or “Arutheos.” It is not a description of an action, quality, or general thing, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:25. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide further meaning or significance beyond naming the individual. Its precise reference in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in the list.

Aser, also rendered Asir, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named figure or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or ordinary object. The name occurs 42 times across 40 verses, from Genesis through Ezekiel, with many occurrences in Numbers and Joshua. Its precise identity in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy, but the word itself functions as a personal or group name, not as a general descriptive term.

This Greek LXX noun means “going away” or “departure.” It refers plainly to leaving or moving away, rather than naming a person, place, or action of arrival. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 7:10. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be stated responsibly. Its basic meaning remains the act or event of going away, with the surrounding context determining what departure is meant.

Bakbakar, also rendered “Vakvakar,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name should therefore be treated as a designation without assigning it an additional meaning beyond its identified form. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:15. Its precise significance in that reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.h: To Profane or Treat as Common
e.t: This verb means to profane—to treat something holy as ordinary, dishonored, or unfit for sacred use. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an action that violates the distinction between what is devoted to God and what is common. The word occurs 75 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, especially in Ezekiel and Leviticus. Its use may concern holy things, God’s name, worship, or conduct that brings dishonor to what is sacred.

Βηθαχαρμ is a proper name referring to a place or locality known as “Bēthacharm” or “Vithakharm.” It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a specific geographic designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:14. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further, but its lexical function is clear: it identifies a named location.

This noun refers to the plant called “butomus” or “flowering rush.” It is a specific plant name rather than a description of an action, feeling, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, so its use is limited to those two passages. The word identifies the plant itself; the precise significance of each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective describes someone who is “slow of tongue”—not quick or fluent in speaking. It refers to a limitation or slowness in speech rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 4:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points plainly to difficulty or slowness in expressing oneself verbally.

This Greek LXX verb means “honour”: it describes treating someone as worthy of respect and esteem. As a verb, it expresses what a person does toward another rather than naming a person or thing. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:17. Its central sense is clear, though the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Gotholia is a proper name, rendered as “Gotholia.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 13 times, in 13 verses across 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles. The available information establishes the name’s identity and use as a personal designation, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in any particular passage.

This word is a proper name rendered as “Daidan” or “Thethan.” It identifies a named person or people in the Greek Old Testament tradition, rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs eight times across seven Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its precise referent depends on the passage where it appears, but its basic function remains that of a personal or group name. The two supplied forms represent the same named entity in this LXX corpus.

Demna, also known as Themna, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This LXX word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 21:35. Its lexical meaning is therefore the name itself, not a broader concept or spiritual quality. The specific referent of the name depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “make clear”: to bring something into understanding so that its meaning, truth, or purpose can be recognized. It describes clarifying or revealing something rather than leaving it hidden or uncertain. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages in Exodus, Psalms, Isaiah, Daniel, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being made clear and the surrounding context.

gl: draw a boundary through; divide by limits
d: draw a boundary through; divide by limits

e.t: This Greek Old Testament verb means “draw a boundary through” or “divide by limits.” It describes separating or marking things by a defined line, border, or limit rather than leaving them undifferentiated. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages concerning boundaries, divisions, and separating one area from another. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being divided or bounded there.

This adverb means “double” or “in two ways.” It describes something done, understood, or presented with two aspects rather than only one. Its function is to qualify another word or statement by indicating this doubled character. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 23:11. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the precise force of the word in that sentence must be determined from its context.

This adjective describes something marked by the deepest or greatest sorrow, expressing the idea of being “most mournful.” It is a strong description of grief or lamentation rather than a general word for sadness. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself emphasizes an especially sorrowful condition or expression.

This is a proper name rendered “Eber” or “Ever,” referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, appearing seven times in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is the identification of Eber himself; the surrounding verse determines what is being said about him.

This Greek LXX noun means “food,” referring to something prepared or provided for eating. It names nourishment in ordinary human life, whether offered in a household setting or spoken of as part of daily provision. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including several occurrences in Genesis 27. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: edible food or a meal-related provision. The surrounding passage determines the particular kind of food intended in any given verse.

This adjective describes someone who vindicates a wrong or avenges an offense. It refers to a person who acts to secure justice by answering wrongdoing, rather than merely observing it. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs three times, including places rendered “avenger.” Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and who is being defended or opposed.

This verb means “fit”: it describes the act of making something suitable or properly joined. As a verb, it points to an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:26. The word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, so its normal meaning can be stated without assigning details from context.

This Greek LXX verb means “devise” or “plan”: it describes forming an intention or working out a course of action in the mind. It can refer to planning something that will be done, whether the purpose is good or harmful; the surrounding passage determines that moral direction. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is broader than one particular situation.

This adjective means “of three strands” or “threefold”: something involving three strands or three parts. It describes a three-part structure rather than something single or doubled. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ecclesiastes 4:12. Its basic sense identifies the number and arrangement of the strands; the surrounding verse is needed to explain how that description functions there.

This noun means “going out”—the act or movement of departing from a place. It describes movement away rather than a person or an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Samuel 15:20. The word’s exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the outward act of going out. It is therefore a straightforward noun describing departure from one location toward another.

To glean means to gather what remains after a harvest, especially by collecting overlooked grain or produce. This verb expresses an action rather than a person, place, or quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 2:9; however, no verse text is available here to explain its particular use in that passage. Its central sense is simply gathering leftover harvest.

This adjective describes something pleasing or delightful—something that gives enjoyment or is agreeable to experience. It presents the quality itself rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:39. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider setting, but its ordinary meaning is the positive quality of being enjoyable, attractive, or agreeable.

This noun means “agent”: a person acting on behalf of another, such as a representative entrusted with carrying out someone else’s business or authority. It is a role word, so its precise force in a sentence depends on whose interests the agent represents and what task has been assigned. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees. This limited usage supports the straightforward sense of an appointed agent or representative rather than a broad description of any person who acts.

This Greek LXX verb means “work” or “perform”: it describes carrying out an activity, task, or deed. It can refer broadly to labor or to accomplishing something that is required or undertaken. The word occurs 104 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic sense is broad rather than limited to one kind of labor. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “give thanks” or “thank.” It describes expressing gratitude, whether directed toward someone or offered as thanks. As a verb, it names the action of thanking rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the act of giving thanks.

This adverb describes doing something sweetly or gladly—that is, with pleasantness, willingness, or joy. It tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across Esther, Proverbs, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Depending on the sentence, it can express a willing response, a pleasant manner, or cheerful acceptance. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains a positive and willing manner of action.

This adjective describes someone as lusty or mad after women—strongly driven by sexual desire toward women. It portrays an intense, uncontrolled craving rather than a neutral description of attraction. In the Greek LXX, the word occurs once, in Jeremiah 5:8, so its precise force there belongs to that verse’s surrounding context. Its central meaning remains a description of excessive sexual desire directed toward women.

Iazer, also written Iazir, is a proper name used for a named place in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object; it identifies a particular location. The name occurs 15 times in the LXX corpus, especially in Numbers and Joshua, and appears in passages concerning Israel’s territorial setting. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Iethebaal, also rendered Iethevaal, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 16:31. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name itself can be explained clearly, while the person’s role and the passage’s significance must be understood from that verse and its wider setting.

“Ierousa,” also rendered “Ierusa,” is a proper name used to identify a specific person or place. It is not a general description or action word, but a name that points to one particular named subject in the passage. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Kings 15:33 and 2 Chronicles 27:1. The exact referent and significance of the name in either verse depend on the surrounding passage.

Iramael, also rendered Iramel, is a proper name identifying a person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 24:29. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name itself can be explained only as a personal designation, not by assigning it a broader quality, action, or spiritual meaning. Its role in that passage depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective means “like a star,” describing something by comparing it with a star. It presents a star-like quality or appearance rather than naming a star itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 17:5. The available lexical meaning is clear, while the precise force of the comparison in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its use is therefore best understood as a descriptive word that points the reader toward the recognizable character or appearance of a star.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iōachaz” or “Ioakhaz.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in 2 Chronicles, from 2 Chronicles 25:17 through 36:4. The name’s precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage, since the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

This word means “bag” or “pouch,” a noun for a small container used to carry something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Samuel 17. Its meaning is therefore concrete and practical rather than describing a person, action, or inward quality. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain exactly what is carried or how the container functions in each occurrence.

Kallisthenes, also rendered Kallisthenis, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:33. The available lexical information identifies the name itself, but the verse text is not provided here, so no further description of this person or the event can be drawn from the name alone.

This word means “beetle,” the name of a small crawling insect. It is a noun, so it identifies the creature itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs once, in Habakkuk 2:11. The precise significance of its use in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text, but its basic meaning is the insect named here.

Kariathbaal, also rendered Kariathvaal, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Joshua, where it functions as the name of a particular location. The name occurs in Joshua 15:60, 18:14, and 18:15. These references establish its use as a place-name, while the name itself does not provide a broader definition.

This Greek LXX verb means “swallow” or “consume”—to take something down so that it is no longer outside the one consuming it. It can describe literal swallowing, but its normal sense may also portray something being completely taken in or overwhelmed. The word occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and once in the deuterocanonical writings, so its basic idea is consistent across a range of passages. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being swallowed or consumed.

This verb means “shine upon”: to cast light onto someone or something. It describes light falling on its object rather than merely existing nearby. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 1 Maccabees, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. The exact force in either passage depends on what is receiving the light and how the sentence uses the verb.

This word means “bowls,” referring to open vessels used to hold or present something. It is a noun describing the objects themselves, not an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 8:27. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how these bowls function there, but the word’s basic meaning remains ordinary bowls or similar vessels.

This Greek LXX verb means “conceive,” describing the beginning of pregnancy or becoming pregnant. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Isaiah 59, so its recorded use is limited to that passage. Understanding its precise force in either verse requires the surrounding verse text.

This noun refers to a "populace" or "population": a group of people considered together. In the Greek Old Testament and its related deuterocanonical books, it is a broad, frequently used term for people collectively rather than for one individual. Its precise reference may be a people generally or a defined population, depending on the sentence. It occurs 1,864 times in this Greek LXX corpus, showing that it is a normal word for speaking about people as a whole.

Leasamys, also rendered Leasamis, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 5:16. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or significance beyond identifying this individual by name.

This noun means “flax straw,” referring to the dry stalks left after flax has been processed. It names a physical plant material rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Joshua 2:6. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the material is being described there.

Maasa is a proper name, preserved as “Maasa” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal or place-name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 19:26. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its lexical role is clear: it is a named designation, not a general description.

This LXX word describes someone or something as “blessed” or “prosperous”—a condition of well-being, favor, or good fortune. It can function as an adjective describing a person or condition, and it may also be used as a noun for one who is blessed. The word occurs 60 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with “blessed” as its predominant English rendering. Its broad use includes descriptions found in Genesis, Job, Psalms, and other books.

Mattari is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description or action word. The name occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, both instances being counted within 1 Samuel 10:21. Because no verse text or wider passage is provided here, its precise referent in that passage cannot be explained further; the secure lexical meaning is simply the name “Mattari.”

gl: with a great name; giving glory
d: with a great name; giving glory

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something associated with a great name, or as giving glory. Its central idea is greatness expressed through a name or through bringing glory. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs once, at Jeremiah 39:19. The surrounding sentence determines exactly what it describes, but its basic meaning remains connected with having a great name or giving glory.

This word means “nevertheless”: it marks a contrast, showing that what follows remains true despite something just mentioned or expected. As a particle, it works as a connecting word rather than naming a person, thing, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Psalm 38:7. Its basic force is concise and connective: it acknowledges a preceding point while introducing an opposing or qualifying statement. The exact emphasis in Psalm 38:7 depends on the surrounding verse text and passage.

Mergab, also rendered “Mergav,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 5:14. The available lexical information preserves the name but does not provide an additional definition or explain its role in that verse. Its precise significance there therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the person or designation to which the name refers.

This Greek LXX adverb means “while not once; never yet.” It expresses that something has not happened even once up to a stated point, or that an action has never occurred. Thus, it strengthens a negative statement by emphasizing both absence and time. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “memory”: the recalling or keeping in mind of a person, event, or matter. It refers to what is remembered rather than to the act of speaking or writing about it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 15 times, showing a recurring idea connected with human remembrance. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains memory or remembrance. The word appears across Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees.

This adjective means “wet with unguent,” describing something covered or moistened with an ointment, perfume, or other scented substance. It identifies a physical condition rather than an action or a person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided. Its precise force in 3 Maccabees 4:6 depends on the sentence where it appears.

Namessias is a proper name identifying an individual. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship, so its meaning is primarily the person’s name rather than a general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 9:20. The available lexical definition gives the name itself, “Namessias,” without an additional meaning or explanation of its name origin.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Nauē” or “Nai.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 30 times, with most occurrences in the Old Testament books and one in Sirach. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily the person it identifies; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role in any particular passage.

Xerxes, also rendered Kserksis, is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Daniel 9:1. The word itself identifies the person named there rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the personal name Xerxes.

This Greek LXX noun means “loud crying”—a strong, audible expression of distress or lament. It refers to the crying itself rather than describing the person who cries. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, once in Isaiah 15:8 and once in Zephaniah 1:10. Those references establish its limited but consistent use as a term for an intense public or audible cry. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the specific situation in either passage.

This Greek LXX word means “on the other side.” It describes a place or position across from, beyond, or opposite something, and it can function either as an adverb or as a preposition. The word is used 101 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, often for locations separated by a boundary, region, or body of water. Its exact nuance in a particular passage depends on what place or object the surrounding sentence identifies. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L710280:identity; p03:word:lxx:L710280:occurrences]

This noun means “standing round” or a “crowd standing round,” describing people gathered around something or someone. It points to a surrounding group rather than to one individual. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Ezekiel and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central idea remains a circle or crowd gathered around. [p03:word:lxx:L710389:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710389:occurrences]

This Greek LXX verb means to attain length of days—to live a long life or be long-lived. It describes the outcome of extended life rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 11:21, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: continued life over many days, understood as a lengthened lifespan. [p03:word:lxx:L710626:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710626:occurrences]

This verb means “hardened beforehand.” It describes hardening that has already taken place before the relevant event or situation. As a verb, it presents this prior hardening as an action or condition rather than as a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:1. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

Sabaim is a proper name, also rendered Savem. It identifies a particular person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Nehemiah 7:59. The available wording gives the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to determine more about the person or place it identifies. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the proper name Sabaim, with Savem as an approved alternate rendering.

Sammaus, also rendered Sammafs, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:41. The available lexical meaning identifies it only as the name itself, so its precise referent and significance must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone. This name belongs to the Old Testament Greek corpus and should not be treated as an ordinary vocabulary term.

Sarada, also rendered Saratha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Numbers 34:8, identifying a person or place by name. The available lexical meaning is limited to the name itself, so its precise identity and significance must be understood from the surrounding passage. This LXX name should be kept distinct from similarly rendered names in other biblical language traditions.

Saphphan, also rendered Saffan, is a proper name identifying a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, all within five verses of 2 Kings 22, from 2 Kings 22:3 through 2 Kings 22:14. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is chiefly its identification of that individual. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the person’s specific role in each occurrence.

This noun means “lance,” a weapon used for thrusting or striking. It names a physical implement rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in passages from Numbers, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, and Joel. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a lance or spear-like weapon.

This word means “today” or “present”. It is an adverb that points to the current day or the time at hand. It can focus attention on what is happening now rather than on a past or future time. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 269 times, showing that it is a common way to mark the time being discussed. Its exact force in a sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains the present time.

This verb means “overthrow” or “upset”: it describes overturning something or disrupting its established position. It is an action word, expressing what someone or something does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 10:18. The precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on bringing something down, overturning it, or upsetting it.
